o: Among the indices holding prime values, return the largest index gap (0 if only one prime exists). Values are bounded by 100, so the set of primes involved is tiny: precompute primality for 1..100 once. In Example 1 primes sit at indices 1, 3, 4 → answer 4 − 1 = 3. In Example 2 the only prime is at index 2 → answer 0. Then a single scan recording the first and last prime indices gives the answer.
k: Values ≤ 100: sieve (or hardcode) primality up to 100, then the problem is just first-vs-last occurrence.
Answer = lastPrimeIndex − firstPrimeIndex, which is 0 when a single prime exists.

a.i: Build a boolean isPrime table for 0..100 with the Eratosthenes sieve. Sweep nums once, updating the first index where a prime was seen and the most recent prime index; their difference is the maximum distance, since extremes maximize any gap.
s: Scan nums, recording firstPrime (first index with a prime value) and lastPrime (latest such index).
a.t: O(n + P√P) with P = 100 — the sieve is constant work; the scan is linear.
a.sp: O(P) = O(1) for the primality table.

a.i: Skip the sieve and test each value for primality on the fly by checking divisors up to its square root (values ≤ 100 need at most 9 checks). Slightly more work per element but needs no preprocessing and is easy to adapt if the value bound grows moderately.
s: Write isPrime(x): false for x < 2; otherwise test divisors d from 2 while d*d ≤ x.
Scan nums, tracking first and last prime indices as before.
a.t: O(n·√V) with V ≤ 100 — constant-factor heavier than the sieve but still linear.

w: Either works; the sieve is the cleaner habit when many primality queries are made. Key observations to voice: the maximum gap is always between the first and last prime (any interior pair is closer), and 1 is not prime. Pitfalls: treating 0/1 as prime, and forgetting the single-prime case returns 0 (which falls out naturally). Follow-up: if values were up to 10⁹ you would need Miller–Rabin or trial division up to √V per element.
